The Executive Branch. One of the three coordinate powers of the United States federal government, headed by the President and charged with enforcing the laws Congress enacts. It comprises the President, Cabinet, federal agencies, and bureaucracy that carry out the nation's day-to-day governance. The separation of this power from legislative and judicial authority is foundational to American constitutional design.

The Executive Branch is headed by the President, who is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and chief executive officer of the federal government. It includes the Cabinet, a group of department heads from State, Defense, Treasury, Interior, and other major departments who advise the President and manage major administrative functions. The branch enforces federal laws, negotiates treaties subject to Senate ratification, and appoints federal judges and senior officials. It is subject to checks by Congress, which can override vetoes, impeach, and control funding, and also by the courts, which review executive action for constitutionality. The President can veto legislation, invoke executive orders, and delegate authority to agencies and subordinates. The Executive Branch grew dramatically in size and scope during the twentieth century, particularly under Franklin D. Roosevelt during the Depression and World War Two. It includes the President's staff, the White House Office, and specialized agencies like the Office of Management and Budget that advise and support executive decision-making. Presidents have assumed broader powers over time through executive orders, national emergencies, and military actions, sometimes sparking constitutional disputes with Congress. Modern presidents command a vast bureaucratic apparatus managing everything from social security to environmental regulation, making the Executive Branch the largest of the three branches in actual staffing. It connects to the principle of separation of powers, which distributes federal authority among three branches; checks and balances, the system by which each branch constrains the others with Congress checking executive power through oversight and appropriation; the legislative branch as the co-equal branch that makes law; the judicial branch whose courts review executive action and decide constitutional limits on presidential power; the President as the elected head of the Executive Branch; and impeachment as the House power to charge a President with high crimes and misdemeanors.
